title: Winning the AI Race Is a Fool's Errand. Find Your Lane Instead.
author: Salinas, Joel
summary: Building on an analogy from Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch, this piece argues that leaders have fundamentally mis-categorized AI adoption as a race — with a start, finish line, and single winning path — when it actually functions more like electricity: fragmented, multi-source infrastructure that every serious organization eventually generates, imports, and exports some of, never single-sourced and never 'won.' The stakes of this category error are documented with real numbers: MIT's Project NANDA found 95% of organizations see zero return on generative AI investment, and the share of companies abandoning most of their AI initiatives jumped from 17% to 42% in one year. The author traces the failure to its root — IBM found 64% of CEOs invest in AI out of fear of falling behind rather than a clear use case, and McKinsey found 88% of companies use AI in some function but only 39% see any bottom-line impact — arguing that fear-driven, target-less adoption produces exactly this kind of activity without results. His practical prescription is to pick a narrow 'lane' of real expertise (his own being leadership plus two specific tools) rather than trying to master any meaningful slice of the more than 51,000 AI tools now available, and to bring in specialists for everything outside that lane rather than spreading thin. The piece closes on its sharpest reframe: AI is a 'how,' never a 'why' — you will never hit a target you don't have, so aiming has to come before adopting.
points: Reframes AI adoption using Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch's electricity analogy: infrastructure that fragments and diversifies by necessity, never a single winner-take-all race.
Cites hard numbers on the cost of the race mentality: MIT found 95% of organizations get zero ROI on generative AI, and companies abandoning AI initiatives jumped from 17% to 42% in one year.
Traces the root cause to fear rather than strategy: 64% of CEOs (IBM survey) invest in AI out of fear of falling behind before understanding its value.
Practical prescription: with 51,000+ AI tools now available, pick one lane of genuine expertise and bring in specialists for the rest, rather than chasing tool-hoarding breadth.
quotes: AI is not a race. A race has a start, a finish line, and one path to run, and AI adoption has none of the three. Trying to win it wastes time, which is part of why 95% of organizations see zero return on generative AI.

No serious country would accept it, he said. Energy fragments because it has to, so every country imports some, exports some, and makes its own. He thinks AI ends up the same way, less a winner-take-all sprint and more like the power grid.
IBM surveyed 2,000 CEOs in 2025, and 64% admitted they invest in technology out of fear of falling behind, before they understand the value it brings.
McKinsey's 2025 research found 88% of companies now use AI in at least one function, but only 39% see any bottom-line impact. Almost everyone is using it. Almost no one aimed it first.
AI is a how, never a why. It's electricity, not the destination. Electricity doesn't tell you where to drive, it just powers the car once you know. You will never hit a target you don't have.
